h: Shabbat Truth, Yaakov's Exile and the Dream of Truth
The Awe of Shabbat and the World of Truth

p: — The statement of the Sages, of blessed memory
— "The awe of Shabbat is upon him,"
— is mentioned with regard to his telling the truth,
— that he is afraid to lie on Shabbat.
— For this is the root of the holiness of Shabbat:
— that the aspect of truth shines forth in it.
— For Shabbat is a semblance of the World to Come,
— while this world is "the world of falsehood,"
— I was in a world of falsehood, etc.;
— but now that I am in the world of truth,
— And this is the division between Yaakov and Esav:
— and so too he was named Esav,
— "Here is the falsehood (shav) that I created in My world."
— And Yaakov took as his portion
— as it says: "Grant truth to Yaakov."

paragraphs.text: Mishnah Demai 4:1: “One who buys produce from someone who is not trusted on tithes and forgot to tithe it may ask him on Shabbat and eat on his word. Once it grows dark at the close of Shabbat, he may not eat until he tithes.” The Mishnah gives only the ruling; the words Rav Tzadok quotes, “the awe of Shabbat is upon him,” are the Yerushalmi's reason for it (next note).

paragraphs.text: Parallel: R. Tzvi Elimelech Shapira of Dinov, Bnei Yissaschar, Shabbatot 3:6: “We learned: one who buys produce from someone not trusted on tithes and forgot to tithe it may ask him on Shabbat and eat on his word. They gave the reason: even an am ha'aretz, suspected of eating untithed produce, which carries the death penalty, is afraid to lie on Shabbat, for the awe of Shabbat is upon him and he tells the truth. This is surprising, for even on Shabbat one may not eat with an am ha'aretz, since on Shabbat too he is suspected of eating untithed produce, and in that the awe of Shabbat is not upon him; yet about not lying and telling the truth we do say that the awe of Shabbat is upon him. It seems to me that the attribute ‘and truth’ is the seventh of the Thirteen Attributes, and it shines on the seventh day as the light of the faces of Israel. For this attribute is the light of the King's face, and it lights up the faces of Israel, the children of kings, and they are afraid to lie. ... From this you will understand what the Sages said of the town whose name was Kushta, where no one died before his time: the attribute of truth is the shining of the Face, and ‘in the light of the King's face is life.’ ... And consider further what the Sages said, ‘Yaakov our father did not die,’ for it is written, ‘Grant truth to Yaakov.’”

paragraphs.text: Parallel: Pri Tzaddik, Kedoshim 11: “At the third meal, which corresponds to Yaakov our father, peace be upon him, whose trait is truth, as it says, ‘Grant truth to Yaakov’ ... On Shabbat, when the Blessed One has rest from His world through Israel, the holiness of Yaakov our father, peace be upon him, shines in them. And it is stated in the Yerushalmi (Demai, chapter 4), concerning one who asks him and eats on his word, that even an am ha'aretz has the awe of Shabbat upon him and cannot tell a lie. ... For Yaakov took in all the good, and therefore he did not die, and Esav took in all the evil. This is the division of the worlds of which the Sages spoke: this one took the World to Come, and that one this world, which is the world of falsehood. And so it is stated in Bereishis Rabbah (Toldos) that he is called Esav, ‘here is vanity’; and he also hates all creatures, as it says there in Bereishis Rabbah on the verse ‘you hated blood,’ that he hates the blood of a man in his body.”

h: Yaakov's Exile and the Unwitting Killer

p: — And it is stated in the Tanchuma (beginning of this parashah):
— goes into exile to the cities of refuge, etc.;
— and Yaakov our father went into exile to Charan,
— fleeing for his life, and he was afraid, etc.
— Once the Holy One, blessed be He, saw him
— He revealed Himself to him in a dream."
— what does Yaakov's exile have to do
— And what is the point of His revealing Himself to him,
— the Holy One, blessed be He, in a dream,
— that the serpent brought death into the world
— and this is the trait of Esav,
— "You hated the blood of a man in his body,"
— that is, the kelipah of murder.
— And Yaakov is a chariot for the letter vav,
— which is the letter of truth
— at the beginning of Parashas Vayikra).
— the corruption of falsehood to such a degree,
לִפְנֵי הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא עַל חֶטְאוֹ.
— before the Holy One, blessed be He, over his sin.
— who had already made the blemish of death
— and he went out like one who deceives the Mind on High
— God, may He be blessed, judged him
— as the Sages, of blessed memory, said
— that he argued: "I did not know,
— and I had never in my life seen a slain person;
שֶׁאֲנִי מַכֵּהוּ בְּאֶבֶן וְהוּא מֵת כּוּלֵּי
— that if I struck him with a stone he would die? etc."
— And because of this he was sentenced to exile,
— to be "a wanderer and a fugitive," etc.

paragraphs.text: Midrash Tanchuma, Vayetzei 1:1: “One who kills a person unintentionally goes into exile to the cities of refuge ... and Yaakov our father went into exile to Charan, fleeing for his life, and he was afraid lest the wicked Esav his brother kill him. Once the Holy One, blessed be He, saw him in great distress, He revealed Himself to him in a dream.” Rav Tzadok's first “etc.” passes over the list of the six cities; his second passes over the stated object of Yaakov's fear, “that the wicked Esav would kill him.”

paragraphs.text: Zohar I 143a (Toldot): “Once he said ‘before Hashem,’ at that very moment the Throne of Glory of the Holy One, blessed be He, shook, and it said: Shall the serpent then come out of those curses, and Yaakov be left in them?” When Yitzchak said he would bless Esav “before Hashem,” the Throne of Glory shook. Two paragraphs later (Zohar, Toldot 19:141) the Zohar says: “Yaakov came with wisdom and misled his father, in order to bring blessings upon the world” — measure for measure against the serpent.

paragraphs.text: Sanhedrin 97a: “Once I chanced upon a certain place whose name was Kushta, and they did not deviate in their words, and no one there died before his time ... They told her: She is not here. His two sons died ... ‘Please, leave our place, and do not provoke death among these people.’” In a town called Kushta (“Truth”) no one lied and no one died before his time. Rav Tavut said his wife was not home, out of modesty, and his two sons died; the townspeople asked him to leave so as not to bring death upon them. Rav Tzadok's point: even a permitted deviation from truth, in a place of truth, brought death and exile.

h: The Dream That Confirmed His Truth

p: — Over this he was deeply embittered,
— and his heart cried out to Hashem:
— rescue my soul from a lying lip" —
— that his soul not be judged
— for this as a lying lip.
— so that it becomes clear that it was done in truth.
— And about this the Midrash said:
— "Once the Holy One, blessed be He, saw him
— He revealed Himself to him in a dream."
נִתְבָּרֵר לוֹ לְיַעֲקֹב אָבִינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם
— it became clear to Yaakov our father, peace be upon him,
— that he had not blemished the trait of truth at all.
— For as is known, it is impossible
— for a dream to be without idle matters
— yet to Yaakov our father, peace be upon him,
— the Holy One, blessed be He, appeared in a dream
כְּמוֹ שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר וְהִנֵּה ה' נִצָּב עָלָיו.
— as it says: "And behold, Hashem stood over him."
— From this he was confident in himself
— that he cleaves to the trait of truth
— and had certainly not blemished it at all in this.
— And as the Sages, of blessed memory, said
עַל מַה שֶּׁנֶּאֱמַר בָּא אָחִיךָ בְּמִרְמָה
— on the verse "Your brother came with guile":
— that Yaakov should take the blessings

h: Shabbat-Eve Dreams and Rabbi Meir's Purse

p: וְהִנֵּה אִיתָא בַּגְּמָרָא (יוֹמָא פג עַמּוּד ב)
— Now it is stated in the Gemara (Yoma 83b)
— that Rabbi Meir said to a certain man:
— that is, dreams of Shabbat night,
— Yet on the face of it, according to what was said above,
— the dreams of Shabbat, more truthful,
— in keeping with the root of the holiness of the time of Shabbat.
— on the contradiction between the verses
— "In a dream I speak with him"
— and it is written "and dreams speak falsehood":
— here it is through an angel,
— And the Chiddushei Aggados of the Maharsha observed
— that this dream was certainly not
— through an angel, telling him to steal;
— and if it came through the opposite,
— how did it hit upon the truth,
— that Rabbi Meir had hidden his purse there?
— through the spirit of his father,
— who counseled him to steal on Shabbat
— and to desecrate it by digging in his grave.
— And for this man the awe of Shabbat was of no avail,
— for he was not a Shabbat observer;
— and even so he hit upon the truth
— in his wickedness, through counsel of falsehood.
— the point of truth shines upon him
— in that he is afraid to lie.
— And in proportion to the soul, according to its level,
— so does he have a sensitivity
— so that he has an inclination
— which is a semblance of the World to Come,

paragraphs.text: Yoma 83b: “Rabbi Meir did not entrust his purse to him; he went and placed it at the grave of the man's father. It was shown to the man in his dream: Come, take the purse that is lying at the head of that man. The next day he told them ... They said to him: Dreams of bei shimshei have no substance.” R. Meir would not leave his purse with the innkeeper Kidor, whose name marked him as wicked, and hid it at the grave of the man's father. Rav Tzadok's reading, that the dream came from the father's spirit, rests on this detail: the purse was hidden in the father's grave.

paragraphs.text: Rashi on Yoma 83b: “Bei shimshei: of Friday nights. Have no substance: because a person at rest muses and sees dreams. And he meant to put him off, so that he would not go and take it.” Bei shimshei means Friday nights; such dreams lack substance because a resting person muses and dreams. Rashi adds that R. Meir meant to put the man off.

paragraphs.text: Maharsha, Chiddushei Aggadot on Yoma 83b: “According to what they said in Perek HaRo'eh, that a true dream comes through an angel and a false dream through a demon, this dream was certainly not through an angel, to tell his son to steal this purse of Rabbi Meir; nor was it through a demon, for it was true.” The Maharsha's question is exactly as Rav Tzadok reports it. His answer is different: the dream followed the man's own thoughts, since all day he had been plotting how to get R. Meir's money. Rav Tzadok answers instead that the father's spirit counseled him.
